$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡xy)\,j \\  & =\frac{y}{xy}\,i+\frac{x}{xy}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{1}{y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y={t}^{2}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2t\,j) \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{t}-\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\  & =\frac{2-t\operatorname{tan}⁡t}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124094 :answer-field/correct "answer-28207432-84ed-53b8-96d3-f43fe1450b2c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-683e544e-ffb7-547d-87ef-b5301c6dac41" "answer-28207432-84ed-53b8-96d3-f43fe1450b2c" "answer-99330b27-129d-50df-97de-421d0fe9607b" "answer-21d33325-0f7c-59d5-9622-3be484ea7f04" "answer-fa4236d2-abd7-5e33-9757-638b2e5b9cc5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-683e544e-ffb7-547d-87ef-b5301c6dac41" :answer/id #uuid "683e544e-ffb7-547d-87ef-b5301c6dac41" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2-t\operatorname{sec}⁡t}{t}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-28207432-84ed-53b8-96d3-f43fe1450b2c" :answer/id #uuid "28207432-84ed-53b8-96d3-f43fe1450b2c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2-t\operatorname{tan}⁡t}{t}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-99330b27-129d-50df-97de-421d0fe9607b" :answer/id #uuid "99330b27-129d-50df-97de-421d0fe9607b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2t+1}{{t}^{2}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-21d33325-0f7c-59d5-9622-3be484ea7f04" :answer/id #uuid "21d33325-0f7c-59d5-9622-3be484ea7f04" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{{t}^{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡t+1}{{t}^{2}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fa4236d2-abd7-5e33-9757-638b2e5b9cc5" :answer/id #uuid "fa4236d2-abd7-5e33-9757-638b2e5b9cc5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{{t}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡t+2}{{t}^{2}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-240fc49a-d022-5d2c-b6ad-58058500b98b" :question/id #uuid "240fc49a-d022-5d2c-b6ad-58058500b98b" :question/math-academy-id "q-95051" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)={x}^{4}-{y}^{4}$ and $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}-{y}^{4})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{4}-{y}^{4})\,j \\  & =4{x}^{3}\,i-4{y}^{3}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =4{cos}^{3}⁡t\,i-4{sin}^{3}⁡t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(4{cos}^{3}⁡t\,i-4{sin}^{3}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t-4{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-47babdd0-5f4c-5c9a-9ce1-4d934697545f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-47babdd0-5f4c-5c9a-9ce1-4d934697545f" :answer-field/id #uuid "47babdd0-5f4c-5c9a-9ce1-4d934697545f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-c7da010b-a10a-5868-8d20-e4e46c3b4c9d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c7da010b-a10a-5868-8d20-e4e46c3b4c9d" "answer-4b40ea9e-cf34-5238-9134-0581b982e962" "answer-0c059460-c4c2-55a2-8585-7e51d8edae78" "answer-e85749fe-f788-582a-a8ba-6a6fb947faa2" "answer-47522fd9-62bd-5474-804d-67ac7a770b4b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c7da010b-a10a-5868-8d20-e4e46c3b4c9d" :answer/id #uuid "c7da010b-a10a-5868-8d20-e4e46c3b4c9d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4b40ea9e-cf34-5238-9134-0581b982e962" :answer/id #uuid "4b40ea9e-cf34-5238-9134-0581b982e962" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0c059460-c4c2-55a2-8585-7e51d8edae78" :answer/id #uuid "0c059460-c4c2-55a2-8585-7e51d8edae78" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e85749fe-f788-582a-a8ba-6a6fb947faa2" :answer/id #uuid "e85749fe-f788-582a-a8ba-6a6fb947faa2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4{cos}^{3}⁡t" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-47522fd9-62bd-5474-804d-67ac7a770b4b" :answer/id #uuid "47522fd9-62bd-5474-804d-67ac7a770b4b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4{sin}^{4}⁡t" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124959 :question/problem "If $f(x,y,z)=xy+yz+xz$ and $r(t)=t\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+e\,k,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+yz+xz)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+yz+xz)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy+yz+xz)\,k \\  & =(y+z)\,i+(x+z)\,j+(y+x)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,y={e}^{t},$ and $z=e$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =({e}^{t}+e)\,i+(t+e)\,j+({e}^{t}+t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(e)\,k \\  & =i+{e}^{t}\,j+(0)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(({e}^{t}+e)\,i+(t+e)\,j+({e}^{t}+t)\,k)\cdot (i+{e}^{t}\,j+(0)\,k) \\  & =({e}^{t}+e)\cdot 1+(t+e)\cdot {e}^{t}+({e}^{t}+t)\cdot 0 \\  & ={e}^{t}+e+t{e}^{t}+{e}^{t+1} \\  & ={e}^{t+1}+(1+t){e}^{t}+e.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186122354 :answer-field/correct "answer-88d607c8-fe3c-5a8f-95e2-26b4560aaab5" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3f8c2a6a-498f-5431-bf0a-f09364aeca5b" "answer-2d6b5248-8092-5223-a861-76c990d98151" "answer-88d607c8-fe3c-5a8f-95e2-26b4560aaab5" "answer-55795f5b-54c2-5a78-8f3f-d7bc330a0c55" "answer-9a2dcd24-b4f5-5abd-afe6-bb8c91b06230"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3f8c2a6a-498f-5431-bf0a-f09364aeca5b" :answer/id #uuid "3f8c2a6a-498f-5431-bf0a-f09364aeca5b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2{e}^{t}+2e+t" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2d6b5248-8092-5223-a861-76c990d98151" :answer/id #uuid "2d6b5248-8092-5223-a861-76c990d98151" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{e}^{t+1}+(1+2t){e}^{t}+e" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-88d607c8-fe3c-5a8f-95e2-26b4560aaab5" :answer/id #uuid "88d607c8-fe3c-5a8f-95e2-26b4560aaab5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{e}^{t+1}+(1+t){e}^{t}+e" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-55795f5b-54c2-5a78-8f3f-d7bc330a0c55" :answer/id #uuid "55795f5b-54c2-5a78-8f3f-d7bc330a0c55" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{e}^{t+1}+(t+1){e}^{t}+2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9a2dcd24-b4f5-5abd-afe6-bb8c91b06230" :answer/id #uuid "9a2dcd24-b4f5-5abd-afe6-bb8c91b06230" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{e}^{t+1}+t{e}^{t}+e" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-430b6986-f30c-500a-b5e9-219dd0f3ace5" :question/id #uuid "430b6986-f30c-500a-b5e9-219dd0f3ace5" :question/math-academy-id "q-167463" :question/problem "If $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)$ and $r(t)=t\,i+2t\,j+\frac{1}{t}\,k,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))\,k \\  & =yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\,i+xz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\,j+xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,$ $y=2t$ and $z=\frac{1}{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,j+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,k \\  & =\,i+2\,j-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,j+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,k)\cdot (\,i+2\,j-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,k) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot 2+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-88e49b12-6312-563d-bb5a-a9112af44abf"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\text{ }i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\text{ }j.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,i+\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\frac{\pi }{4}))] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-da5c7c2a-000b-5483-8ada-2cf63e301ba8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124960 :question/problem "Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+3xyz$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},t+1,-t⟩$ at the point $t=1.$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+3xyz),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+3xyz),\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+3xyz)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x+3yz,3xz,3xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2},y=t+1,$ and $z=-t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2({t}^{2})+3(t+1)(-t),3({t}^{2})(-t),3({t}^{2})(t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2}-3{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,1,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨-{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2t,1,-1⟩ \\  & =(-{t}^{2}-3t)\cdot 2t+(-3{t}^{3})\cdot 1+(3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2})\cdot (-1) \\  & =-2{t}^{3}-6{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3}-3{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2} \\  & =-8{t}^{3}-9{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =-8{(1)}^{3}-9{(1)}^{2}=-17.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186122360 :answer-field/correct 17592186122361 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-b98d6bad-fbc9-5978-8040-a1a35d995f54" :question/id #uuid "b98d6bad-fbc9-5978-8040-a1a35d995f54" :question/math-academy-id "q-36234" :question/problem "Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡t,2t⟩$ at the point $t=\pi .$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $y=2t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩ \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{t}+2{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\pi ))] & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{\pi }+2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi  \\  & =2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi .\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e6ea0794-709e-5625-aee2-f32cf13014aa"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e6ea0794-709e-5625-aee2-f32cf13014aa" :answer-field/id #uuid "e6ea0794-709e-5625-aee2-f32cf13014aa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-4bc8881d-ce79-5fa4-94b3-93194df95932" :answer-field/choices ["answer-869d2a2c-eca1-5a81-9c8c-bd38ea652d36" "answer-e898d08a-c5cb-5c48-be98-c6dd2a755c94" "answer-9980bb90-a6ef-51f4-88b3-4812a2e11e8e" "answer-4bc8881d-ce79-5fa4-94b3-93194df95932" "answer-76ff76d1-a44d-5785-aeb6-f49cd08b8d01"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-869d2a2c-eca1-5a81-9c8c-bd38ea652d36" :answer/id #uuid "869d2a2c-eca1-5a81-9c8c-bd38ea652d36" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\pi )" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e898d08a-c5cb-5c48-be98-c6dd2a755c94" :answer/id #uuid "e898d08a-c5cb-5c48-be98-c6dd2a755c94" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-{ln}^{2}⁡(\pi )" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9980bb90-a6ef-51f4-88b3-4812a2e11e8e" :answer/id #uuid "9980bb90-a6ef-51f4-88b3-4812a2e11e8e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2{ln}^{2}⁡(2\pi )" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4bc8881d-ce79-5fa4-94b3-93194df95932" :answer/id #uuid "4bc8881d-ce79-5fa4-94b3-93194df95932" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2{ln}^{2}⁡(\pi )" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-76ff76d1-a44d-5785-aeb6-f49cd08b8d01" :answer/id #uuid "76ff76d1-a44d-5785-aeb6-f49cd08b8d01" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\pi )" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125835 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the function 

$$
f(\mathbf{r}) = f(x,y) = xy^2,
$$

which takes a vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle x(t), y(t) \right\rangle = \left\langle \cos t, \sin t \right\rangle
$$

as input. How do we calculate $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left[f(\mathbf{r}(t))\right]?$

To do this, we use the **multivariable chain rule in vector form**, which states

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left[f(\mathbf{r}(t))\right] = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot \mathbf{r}'(t).
$$

Let's now apply this to our functions. First, we compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(f(x,y)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(f(x,y))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨{y}^{2},2xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\cos t$ and $y=\sin t$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2},2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =-{sin}^{3}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125749 :tutorial/content "We can consider $f(\mathbf{r}(t))$ as the values taken by the function $f$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t).$ So, the derivative 

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))]
$$

can be interpreted as the **rate of change of $f$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t).$**

Furthermore, if $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is a level curve $f(x,y)=c,$ then by the chain rule we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =c \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(f(r(t))) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(c) \\ ∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

From this, we can conclude that the gradient vector $\nabla f$ is orthogonal to every level curve of $f.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125836 :tutorial/content "The chain rule for a function $f(\mathbf{r}),$ where $\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle x_1(t), x_2(t), \ldots, x_m(t) \right\rangle$ is a vector-valued function of $m$ variables, is the same as before:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)
$$

How does this chain rule in vector form relate to the chain rule we have seen before, which states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d f} {\textrm d t} 	= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_1} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm d x_1}{\textrm d t}  
						+ \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_2} \cdot  \dfrac {\textrm d x_2}{\textrm d t} + \dots + \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_m} \cdot  \dfrac {\textrm d x_m}{\textrm d t}?
$$

Let's expand $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)$ to see. Recall that 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t))=⟨\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}},\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}},…,\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)=⟨\frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{dt},\frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{dt},…,\frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{dt}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}},\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}},…,\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{dt},\frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{dt},…,\frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{dt}⟩ \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{\text{d}t}+⋯+\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

They are exactly the same, just different notations!

**Note**: If we replace $\mathbf{r}$ with a single-valued function $g(t),$ we get back the chain rule from single-variable calculus:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(g(t))] & =∇f(g(t))\cdot {g}^{′}(t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124728 :activity/expected-seconds 1320.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡xy)\,j \\  & =\frac{y}{xy}\,i+\frac{x}{xy}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{1}{y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y={t}^{2}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2t\,j) \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{t}-\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\  & =\frac{2-t\operatorname{tan}⁡t}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124094 :answer-field/correct "answer-28207432-84ed-53b8-96d3-f43fe1450b2c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-683e544e-ffb7-547d-87ef-b5301c6dac41" "answer-28207432-84ed-53b8-96d3-f43fe1450b2c" "answer-99330b27-129d-50df-97de-421d0fe9607b" "answer-21d33325-0f7c-59d5-9622-3be484ea7f04" "answer-fa4236d2-abd7-5e33-9757-638b2e5b9cc5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-683e544e-ffb7-547d-87ef-b5301c6dac41" :answer/id #uuid "683e544e-ffb7-547d-87ef-b5301c6dac41" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2-t\operatorname{sec}⁡t}{t}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-28207432-84ed-53b8-96d3-f43fe1450b2c" :answer/id #uuid "28207432-84ed-53b8-96d3-f43fe1450b2c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2-t\operatorname{tan}⁡t}{t}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-99330b27-129d-50df-97de-421d0fe9607b" :answer/id #uuid "99330b27-129d-50df-97de-421d0fe9607b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2t+1}{{t}^{2}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-21d33325-0f7c-59d5-9622-3be484ea7f04" :answer/id #uuid "21d33325-0f7c-59d5-9622-3be484ea7f04" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{{t}^{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡t+1}{{t}^{2}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fa4236d2-abd7-5e33-9757-638b2e5b9cc5" :answer/id #uuid "fa4236d2-abd7-5e33-9757-638b2e5b9cc5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{{t}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡t+2}{{t}^{2}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-240fc49a-d022-5d2c-b6ad-58058500b98b" :question/id #uuid "240fc49a-d022-5d2c-b6ad-58058500b98b" :question/math-academy-id "q-95051" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)={x}^{4}-{y}^{4}$ and $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}-{y}^{4})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{4}-{y}^{4})\,j \\  & =4{x}^{3}\,i-4{y}^{3}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =4{cos}^{3}⁡t\,i-4{sin}^{3}⁡t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(4{cos}^{3}⁡t\,i-4{sin}^{3}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t-4{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-47babdd0-5f4c-5c9a-9ce1-4d934697545f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-47babdd0-5f4c-5c9a-9ce1-4d934697545f" :answer-field/id #uuid "47babdd0-5f4c-5c9a-9ce1-4d934697545f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-c7da010b-a10a-5868-8d20-e4e46c3b4c9d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c7da010b-a10a-5868-8d20-e4e46c3b4c9d" "answer-4b40ea9e-cf34-5238-9134-0581b982e962" "answer-0c059460-c4c2-55a2-8585-7e51d8edae78" "answer-e85749fe-f788-582a-a8ba-6a6fb947faa2" "answer-47522fd9-62bd-5474-804d-67ac7a770b4b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c7da010b-a10a-5868-8d20-e4e46c3b4c9d" :answer/id #uuid "c7da010b-a10a-5868-8d20-e4e46c3b4c9d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4b40ea9e-cf34-5238-9134-0581b982e962" :answer/id #uuid "4b40ea9e-cf34-5238-9134-0581b982e962" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0c059460-c4c2-55a2-8585-7e51d8edae78" :answer/id #uuid "0c059460-c4c2-55a2-8585-7e51d8edae78" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e85749fe-f788-582a-a8ba-6a6fb947faa2" :answer/id #uuid "e85749fe-f788-582a-a8ba-6a6fb947faa2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4{cos}^{3}⁡t" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-47522fd9-62bd-5474-804d-67ac7a770b4b" :answer/id #uuid "47522fd9-62bd-5474-804d-67ac7a770b4b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4{sin}^{4}⁡t" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124959 :question/problem "If $f(x,y,z)=xy+yz+xz$ and $r(t)=t\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+e\,k,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+yz+xz)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+yz+xz)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy+yz+xz)\,k \\  & =(y+z)\,i+(x+z)\,j+(y+x)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,y={e}^{t},$ and $z=e$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =({e}^{t}+e)\,i+(t+e)\,j+({e}^{t}+t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(e)\,k \\  & =i+{e}^{t}\,j+(0)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(({e}^{t}+e)\,i+(t+e)\,j+({e}^{t}+t)\,k)\cdot (i+{e}^{t}\,j+(0)\,k) \\  & =({e}^{t}+e)\cdot 1+(t+e)\cdot {e}^{t}+({e}^{t}+t)\cdot 0 \\  & ={e}^{t}+e+t{e}^{t}+{e}^{t+1} \\  & ={e}^{t+1}+(1+t){e}^{t}+e.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186122354 :answer-field/correct "answer-88d607c8-fe3c-5a8f-95e2-26b4560aaab5" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3f8c2a6a-498f-5431-bf0a-f09364aeca5b" "answer-2d6b5248-8092-5223-a861-76c990d98151" "answer-88d607c8-fe3c-5a8f-95e2-26b4560aaab5" "answer-55795f5b-54c2-5a78-8f3f-d7bc330a0c55" "answer-9a2dcd24-b4f5-5abd-afe6-bb8c91b06230"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3f8c2a6a-498f-5431-bf0a-f09364aeca5b" :answer/id #uuid "3f8c2a6a-498f-5431-bf0a-f09364aeca5b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2{e}^{t}+2e+t" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2d6b5248-8092-5223-a861-76c990d98151" :answer/id #uuid "2d6b5248-8092-5223-a861-76c990d98151" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{e}^{t+1}+(1+2t){e}^{t}+e" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-88d607c8-fe3c-5a8f-95e2-26b4560aaab5" :answer/id #uuid "88d607c8-fe3c-5a8f-95e2-26b4560aaab5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{e}^{t+1}+(1+t){e}^{t}+e" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-55795f5b-54c2-5a78-8f3f-d7bc330a0c55" :answer/id #uuid "55795f5b-54c2-5a78-8f3f-d7bc330a0c55" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{e}^{t+1}+(t+1){e}^{t}+2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9a2dcd24-b4f5-5abd-afe6-bb8c91b06230" :answer/id #uuid "9a2dcd24-b4f5-5abd-afe6-bb8c91b06230" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{e}^{t+1}+t{e}^{t}+e" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-430b6986-f30c-500a-b5e9-219dd0f3ace5" :question/id #uuid "430b6986-f30c-500a-b5e9-219dd0f3ace5" :question/math-academy-id "q-167463" :question/problem "If $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)$ and $r(t)=t\,i+2t\,j+\frac{1}{t}\,k,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))\,k \\  & =yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\,i+xz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\,j+xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,$ $y=2t$ and $z=\frac{1}{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,j+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,k \\  & =\,i+2\,j-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,j+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,k)\cdot (\,i+2\,j-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,k) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot 2+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-88e49b12-6312-563d-bb5a-a9112af44abf"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\text{ }i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\text{ }j.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$

$$

$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\frac{\pi }{4}))] & =0.\end{aligned}

17592186124960 :question/problem "Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+3xyz$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},t+1,-t⟩$ at the point $t=1.$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+3xyz),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+3xyz),\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+3xyz)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x+3yz,3xz,3xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2},y=t+1,$ and $z=-t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2({t}^{2})+3(t+1)(-t),3({t}^{2})(-t),3({t}^{2})(t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2}-3{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,1,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨-{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2t,1,-1⟩ \\  & =(-{t}^{2}-3t)\cdot 2t+(-3{t}^{3})\cdot 1+(3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2})\cdot (-1) \\  & =-2{t}^{3}-6{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3}-3{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2} \\  & =-8{t}^{3}-9{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =-8{(1)}^{3}-9{(1)}^{2}=-17.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186122360 :answer-field/correct 17592186122361 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-b98d6bad-fbc9-5978-8040-a1a35d995f54" :question/id #uuid "b98d6bad-fbc9-5978-8040-a1a35d995f54" :question/math-academy-id "q-36234" :question/problem "Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡t,2t⟩$ at the point $t=\pi .$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $y=2t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩ \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{t}+2{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\pi ))] & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{\pi }+2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi  \\  & =2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi .\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e6ea0794-709e-5625-aee2-f32cf13014aa"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e6ea0794-709e-5625-aee2-f32cf13014aa" :answer-field/id #uuid "e6ea0794-709e-5625-aee2-f32cf13014aa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-4bc8881d-ce79-5fa4-94b3-93194df95932" :answer-field/choices ["answer-869d2a2c-eca1-5a81-9c8c-bd38ea652d36" "answer-e898d08a-c5cb-5c48-be98-c6dd2a755c94" "answer-9980bb90-a6ef-51f4-88b3-4812a2e11e8e" "answer-4bc8881d-ce79-5fa4-94b3-93194df95932" "answer-76ff76d1-a44d-5785-aeb6-f49cd08b8d01"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-869d2a2c-eca1-5a81-9c8c-bd38ea652d36" :answer/id #uuid "869d2a2c-eca1-5a81-9c8c-bd38ea652d36" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\pi )" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e898d08a-c5cb-5c48-be98-c6dd2a755c94" :answer/id #uuid "e898d08a-c5cb-5c48-be98-c6dd2a755c94" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-{ln}^{2}⁡(\pi )" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9980bb90-a6ef-51f4-88b3-4812a2e11e8e" :answer/id #uuid "9980bb90-a6ef-51f4-88b3-4812a2e11e8e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2{ln}^{2}⁡(2\pi )" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4bc8881d-ce79-5fa4-94b3-93194df95932" :answer/id #uuid "4bc8881d-ce79-5fa4-94b3-93194df95932" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2{ln}^{2}⁡(\pi )" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-76ff76d1-a44d-5785-aeb6-f49cd08b8d01" :answer/id #uuid "76ff76d1-a44d-5785-aeb6-f49cd08b8d01" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\pi )" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125835 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the function 

$$
f(\mathbf{r}) = f(x,y) = xy^2,
$$

which takes a vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle x(t), y(t) \right\rangle = \left\langle \cos t, \sin t \right\rangle
$$

as input. How do we calculate $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left[f(\mathbf{r}(t))\right]?$

To do this, we use the **multivariable chain rule in vector form**, which states

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left[f(\mathbf{r}(t))\right] = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot \mathbf{r}'(t).
$$

Let's now apply this to our functions. First, we compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(f(x,y)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(f(x,y))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨{y}^{2},2xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\cos t$ and $y=\sin t$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2},2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =-{sin}^{3}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125749 :tutorial/content "We can consider $f(\mathbf{r}(t))$ as the values taken by the function $f$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t).$ So, the derivative 

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))]
$$

can be interpreted as the **rate of change of $f$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t).$**

Furthermore, if $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is a level curve $f(x,y)=c,$ then by the chain rule we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =c \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(f(r(t))) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(c) \\ ∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

From this, we can conclude that the gradient vector $\nabla f$ is orthogonal to every level curve of $f.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125836 :tutorial/content "The chain rule for a function $f(\mathbf{r}),$ where $\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle x_1(t), x_2(t), \ldots, x_m(t) \right\rangle$ is a vector-valued function of $m$ variables, is the same as before:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)
$$

How does this chain rule in vector form relate to the chain rule we have seen before, which states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d f} {\textrm d t} 	= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_1} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm d x_1}{\textrm d t}  
						+ \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_2} \cdot  \dfrac {\textrm d x_2}{\textrm d t} + \dots + \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_m} \cdot  \dfrac {\textrm d x_m}{\textrm d t}?
$$

Let's expand $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)$ to see. Recall that 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t))=⟨\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}},\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}},…,\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)=⟨\frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{dt},\frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{dt},…,\frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{dt}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}},\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}},…,\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{dt},\frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{dt},…,\frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{dt}⟩ \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{\text{d}t}+⋯+\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

They are exactly the same, just different notations!

**Note**: If we replace $\mathbf{r}$ with a single-valued function $g(t),$ we get back the chain rule from single-variable calculus:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(g(t))] & =∇f(g(t))\cdot {g}^{′}(t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124728 :activity/expected-seconds 1320.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186125249 :question/problem "If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡xy$ and $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$"] [17592186125249 :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y={t}^{2}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

"The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))\,k \\  & =yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\,i+xz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\,j+xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,$ $y=2t$ and $z=\frac{1}{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,j+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,k \\  & =\,i+2\,j-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,j+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,k)\cdot (\,i+2\,j-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,k) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot 2+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-430b6986-f30c-500a-b5e9-219dd0f3ace5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-88e49b12-6312-563d-bb5a-a9112af44abf" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-021b7b63-3816-5a7a-9f77-baf36bf193bb"] [17592186124960 :question/problem "Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+3xyz$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},t+1,-t⟩$ at the point $t=1.$"] [17592186124960 :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+3xyz),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+3xyz),\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+3xyz)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x+3yz,3xz,3xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2},y=t+1,$ and $z=-t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2({t}^{2})+3(t+1)(-t),3({t}^{2})(-t),3({t}^{2})(t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2}-3{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,1,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨-{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2t,1,-1⟩ \\  & =(-{t}^{2}-3t)\cdot 2t+(-3{t}^{3})\cdot 1+(3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2})\cdot (-1) \\  & =-2{t}^{3}-6{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3}-3{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2} \\  & =-8{t}^{3}-9{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =-8{(1)}^{3}-9{(1)}^{2}=-17.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186124960 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] [17592186122360 :answer-field/correct 17592186122361] ["question-b98d6bad-fbc9-5978-8040-a1a35d995f54" :question/id #uuid "b98d6bad-fbc9-5978-8040-a1a35d995f54"] ["question-b98d6bad-fbc9-5978-8040-a1a35d995f54" :question/math-academy-id "q-36234"] ["question-b98d6bad-fbc9-5978-8040-a1a35d995f54" :question/problem "Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡t,2t⟩$ at the point $t=\pi .$"] ["question-b98d6bad-fbc9-5978-8040-a1a35d995f54" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $y=2t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩ \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{t}+2{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\pi ))] & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{\pi }+2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi  \\  & =2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-b98d6bad-fbc9-5978-8040-a1a35d995f54" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-e6ea0794-709e-5625-aee2-f32cf13014aa" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

as input. How do we calculate $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left[f(\mathbf{r}(t))\right]?$

To do this, we use the **multivariable chain rule in vector form**, which states

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left[f(\mathbf{r}(t))\right] = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot \mathbf{r}'(t).
$$

Let's now apply this to our functions. First, we compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(f(x,y)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(f(x,y))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨{y}^{2},2xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\cos t$ and $y=\sin t$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2},2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =-{sin}^{3}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t).

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{3})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{3})\,j \\  & =2x\,i+6{y}^{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\text{ }i+6{e}^{2t}\text{ }j)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\text{ }i+{e}^{t}\text{ }j) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+6{e}^{2t}\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+6{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}

:question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x-x{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x-x{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =(2-{y}^{2})\,i-2xy\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $y=3{t}^{2}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =(2-9{t}^{4})\,i-6{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\,i+6t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =((2-9{t}^{4})\,i-6{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{t}\,i+6t\,j) \\  & =(2-9{t}^{4})\cdot \frac{1}{t}+(-6{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\cdot 6t \\  & =\frac{2}{t}-9{t}^{3}-36{t}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186360544 :question/id #uuid "4eac0cd5-9d30-54ff-89b8-2cfd1b9003d8" :question/math-academy-id "q-95052" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124469 :knowledge-point/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,j \\  & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\pi t$ and $y={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =\pi \,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j)\cdot (\pi \,i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & =-\pi {e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186360545 :question/id #uuid "99c33c9d-4cdd-5e75-a91b-a13201898eee" :question/math-academy-id "q-95054" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124469 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0096e314-e53e-5d9b-9cee-fe34fa3a6379" :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Vector Form of the Chain Rule to a Function of Two Variables"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4e56dc23-76eb-5db9-9fce-e4d36ef6a300" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3({t}^{2}+1)}{t}" :db/id 17592186358426} {:answer/id #uuid "50d39335-f934-5320-9bd6-5f69635a09d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{{t}^{2}{e}^{t}+2}{{e}^{t}}" :db/id 17592186358445} {:answer/id #uuid "7dab4a7a-ef04-5286-8145-c994f7fd0f0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2(t-1)}{t}" :db/id 17592186358847} {:answer/id #uuid "de80fcbe-829a-5dae-a81d-fb3cf700a555" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "t(t-2)" :db/id 17592186359706} {:answer/id #uuid "eb612ba8-e57f-520d-9b63-e9ab14d4e478" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2(t{e}^{t}-1)}{{e}^{t}}" :db/id 17592186359849}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "7dab4a7a-ef04-5286-8145-c994f7fd0f0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2(t-1)}{t}" :db/id 17592186358847} :answer-field/id #uuid "5ed81ec3-d906-5a86-bc7c-31b1ba6834fb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186360140}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})$ and $r(t)={t}^{-2}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{2xy}{x{y}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{2}{y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{-2}$ and $y={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{{t}^{-2}}\,i+\frac{2}{{e}^{t}}\,j \\  & ={t}^{2}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{-2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =-2{t}^{-3}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =({t}^{2}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j)\cdot (-2{t}^{-3}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & =-2({t}^{2})({t}^{-3})+2{e}^{-t}({e}^{t}) \\  & =2-\frac{2}{t} \\  & =\frac{2(t-1)}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186360547 :question/id #uuid "9d03333b-22a3-579a-b479-87085056a6c0" :question/math-academy-id "q-95059"} {:db/id 17592186124470 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id [f(\mathbf r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $\nabla f(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xz\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xz\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xz\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,k \\  & =z\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,i+\frac{xz}{y}\,j+x\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x= t^2,$ $y = t$ and $z= t^3$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & ={t}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+{t}^{4}\,j+{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\,k \\  & =2t\,i+\,j+3{t}^{2}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$

:question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{3})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{3})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{3})\,k \\  & ={y}^{2}\,i+(2xy+{z}^{3})\,j+3y{z}^{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{3},y=1,$ and $z=t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\,i+3{t}^{3}\,j+3{t}^{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =3{t}^{2}i+(0)\,j+\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\,i+3{t}^{3}\,j+3{t}^{2}\,k)\cdot (3{t}^{2}i+(0)\,j+\,k) \\  & =1\cdot 3{t}^{2}+3{t}^{3}\cdot 0+3{t}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =3{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2} \\  & =6{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186360548 :question/id #uuid "a60dcabe-5a9f-584e-9268-2f3213ceda5a" :question/math-academy-id "q-95070" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124470 :knowledge-point/id #uuid $$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $z=2t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =4{sin}^{3}⁡t\,i-4{cos}^{3}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(4{sin}^{3}⁡t\,i-4{cos}^{3}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,k)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\,k) \\  & =4{sin}^{3}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t-4{cos}^{3}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot 2 \\  & =4{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{cos}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}

t, \cos t, t  \right \rangle$ at the point $t=\dfrac \pi 4.$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf r (t)$ is given by $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] .$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z),\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x,-2y,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x = \sin t, y=\cos t,$ and $z=t$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf r(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-1⟩\cdot ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,1⟩ \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-1\cdot 1 \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1 \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\frac{\pi }{4}))] & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-1 \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124960 :question/id #uuid "e234e1ce-e3a5-5460-9b85-a8876cb6e36c" :question/math-academy-id "q-36247" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124471 :knowledge-point/id #uuid curve $r(t)=⟨2t,\sqrt{t}⟩$ at the point $t=9.$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{y},-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2t$ and $y=\sqrt{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},-2⟩\cdot ⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\cdot 2-2\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=9$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(9))] & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186323770 :question/id #uuid "0c3c463e-b1e6-5da9-a9e8-9ab02a63ca2d" :question/math-academy-id "q-36227"} {:db/id 17592186360526 :question/id #uuid point $t=1.$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz),\frac{∂}{∂y}(xyz),\frac{∂}{∂z}(xyz)⟩ \\  & =⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2t,y=\sqrt{t}$ and $z=3t-1$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\sqrt{t}(3t-1),2t(3t-1),2t\sqrt{t}⟩ \\  & =⟨(3t-1)\sqrt{t},6{t}^{2}-2t,2t\sqrt{t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨(3t-1)\sqrt{t},6{t}^{2}-2t,2t\sqrt{t}⟩\cdot ⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},3⟩ \\  & =(3t-1)\sqrt{t}\cdot 2+(6{t}^{2}-2t)\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+2t\sqrt{t}\cdot 3 \\  & =6t\sqrt{t}-2\sqrt{t}+\frac{3{t}^{2}-t}{\sqrt{t}}+6t\sqrt{t} \\  & =12t\sqrt{t}-2\sqrt{t}+\frac{3{t}^{2}-t}{\sqrt{t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =12(1)\sqrt{1}-2\sqrt{1}+\frac{3(1)^{2}-1}{\sqrt{1}} \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186360528 :question/id #uuid "102aa53b-1989-56be-b06a-9a6f6770770c" :question/math-academy-id "q-94888" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124471 :knowledge-point/id #uuid $r(t)=⟨t,4,\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}⟩$ at the point $t=2.$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{z}^{2}+{y}^{3}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{z}^{2}+{y}^{3}),\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{z}^{2}+{y}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨{z}^{2},3{y}^{2},2xz⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,$ $y=4$ and $z=\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨(\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3})^{2},3(4)^{2},2t\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-3,48,2t\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4),\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0,\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-3,48,2t\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}⟩\cdot ⟨1,0,\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}}⟩ \\  & =({t}^{2}-3)\cdot 1+48\cdot 0+2t\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}\cdot \frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}} \\  & ={t}^{2}-3+0+2{t}^{2} \\  & =3{t}^{2}-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(2))] & =3(2)^{2}-3 \\  & =12-3 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186360529 :question/id #uuid "530f5767-4f31-5ef7-a6dd-bdeac420a724" :question/math-academy-id "q-94891"} {:db/id 17592186124593 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124404 :question/id #uuid "c623bb85-401d-5d00-b4a8-cb86570d3304" :question/math-academy-id "e-8282"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cc017b0d-6418-570a-9a5d-57572e4fe70a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124956 :question/id #uuid "ceb16fee-64a8-51ee-a3b7-7009e970259a" :question/math-academy-id "q-36215"} {:db/id 17592186125246 :question/id #uuid "72c15c65-cd14-5a6c-9b4a-a63cd2f705de" :question/math-academy-id "q-94872"} {:db/id 17592186284585 :question/id #uuid "d2df41f1-db14-5e76-bbfb-6cc0c8cd31a4" :question/math-academy-id "q-167497"} {:db/id 17592186284586 :question/id #uuid "15c14f08-def7-5eb6-8ced-3b42bca65403" :question/math-academy-id "q-167498"} {:db/id 17592186323880 :question/id #uuid "fdba027b-12bc-5b22-aa20-f040a6af0b36" :question/math-academy-id "q-37106"} {:db/id 17592186323883 :question/id #uuid "48ca6f9a-7d23-5701-9123-39d54477cf36" :question/math-academy-id "q-37109"} {:db/id 17592186360524 :question/id #uuid "97fd3ba8-8ab5-5d07-adaa-98357dd8d4e1" :question/math-academy-id "q-94873"} {:db/id 17592186360525 :question/id #uuid "f3d7bbdd-6122-519c-8393-02c2402f7ab7" :question/math-academy-id "q-94878"}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating the Derivative at a Point Using the Chain Rule"} {:db/id 17592186124404 :question/id #uuid "c623bb85-401d-5d00-b4a8-cb86570d3304" :question/math-academy-id "e-8282" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186124593 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cc017b0d-6418-570a-9a5d-57572e4fe70a" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating the Derivative at a Point Using the Chain Rule"}] :question/problem "Evaluate $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t}[f(\mathbf r(t))]$ at $t = \pi$ given that
$\nabla f(x,y) = (2y - 1) \, \mathbf i + (2x-1) \, \mathbf j$
and
$\mathbf r (t) = \sin{t} \, \mathbf i + \cos{t} \, \mathbf j.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = (2y - 1) \, \mathbf i + (2x - 1) \, \mathbf j.
$$

First, we substitute $x = \sin{t}$ and $y = \cos{t}$ into $\nabla f(x,y)$ to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)\,i+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1\,i+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1)\,j)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2{sin}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =2({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t = \pi,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\pi ))] & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi +\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\  & =2(1)+0-(-1) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124956 :question/id #uuid "ceb16fee-64a8-51ee-a3b7-7009e970259a" :question/math-academy-id "q-36215" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124593 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cc017b0d-6418-570a-9a5d-57572e4fe70a" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating the Derivative at a Point Using the Chain Rule"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "05130439-f8ad-50ab-88fd-4aef2c512276" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186321194} {:answer/id #uuid "2ab62fb4-96f6-544e-a43f-7c54848d7b96" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186321475} {:answer/id #uuid "2bb77509-e2b1-57fe-aa81-c820e1759f9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186321484} {:answer/id #uuid "dd29a8cb-f3e2-55a6-b61e-7dcb1a986936" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186322877} {:answer/id #uuid "eb8e8763-9fc2-54d7-beb9-a7f164362324" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186322991}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "dd29a8cb-f3e2-55a6-b61e-7dcb1a986936" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186322877} :answer-field/id #uuid "b0f23e9e-f039-5d42-b46f-a3ba271cfc87" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186323513}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]$ at $t=1$ given that
$∇f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,i+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,j$
and
$r(t)=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,i+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=t$ and $y={t}^{2}$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{2(t)}{(t)^{2}+3({t}^{2})}\,i+\frac{3}{(t)^{2}+3({t}^{2})}\,j \\  & =\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2}}\,i+\frac{3}{{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{2t}{4{t}^{2}}\,i+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2t}\,i+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
