{:db/id 17592186125319 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125749 :tutorial/content "We can consider $f(\mathbf{r}(t))$ as the values taken by the function $f$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t).$ So, the derivative 

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))]
$$

can be interpreted as the **rate of change of $f$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t).$**

Furthermore, if $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is a level curve $f(x,y)=c,$ then by the chain rule we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =c \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(f(r(t))) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(c) \\ ∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{'}(t) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

From this, we can conclude that the gradient vector $\nabla f$ is orthogonal to every level curve of $f.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "06350cc4-9c76-53db-a464-43e93f2fcc2f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2652 :tutorial/title "The Derivative as a Rate of Change"} :step/id #uuid "ea045ecb-90e1-5dc8-804d-711207e5f86c" :step/math-academy-id 12681 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125321}} {:db/id 17592186125320 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124470 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124277 :question/id #uuid "033e459e-5148-5e78-ab5c-7e455b06cd64" :question/math-academy-id "e-3695"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "112e3378-bde8-5896-822e-e815bde51501" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124959} {:db/id 17592186125250} {:db/id 17592186284584} {:db/id 17592186360548} {:db/id 17592186360550} {:db/id 17592186360577} {:db/id 17592186360578} {:db/id 17592186360579}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Vector Form of the Chain Rule to a Function of Three Variables"} :step/id #uuid "ef0f7fd7-782e-55cb-8008-f28d770450ed" :step/math-academy-id 12682 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125529}} {:db/id 17592186125321 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124471 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124278 :question/id #uuid "f44b6ea6-694c-5f54-94ee-4c4a699bf4eb" :question/math-academy-id "e-3696"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ea1e5a55-a957-52cd-b693-0e48770672a6" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124960} {:db/id 17592186124961} {:db/id 17592186284587} {:db/id 17592186323770} {:db/id 17592186360526} {:db/id 17592186360527} {:db/id 17592186360528} {:db/id 17592186360529}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Rate of Change of a Multivariable Function at a Point Using the Chain Rule"} :step/id #uuid "cde1eff3-797d-5f65-a385-6296a6f32db3" :step/math-academy-id 12684 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125530}} {:db/id 17592186125528 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125835 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the function 

$$
f(\mathbf{r}) = f(x,y) = xy^2,
$$

which takes a vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle x(t), y(t) \right\rangle = \left\langle \cos t, \sin t \right\rangle
$$

as input. How do we calculate $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left[f(\mathbf{r}(t))\right]?$

To do this, we use the **multivariable chain rule in vector form**, which states

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left[f(\mathbf{r}(t))\right] = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot \mathbf{r}'(t).
$$

Let's now apply this to our functions. First, we compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(f(x,y)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(f(x,y))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨{y}^{2},2xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\cos t$ and $y=\sin t$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨(\operatorname{sin}t)^{2},2(\operatorname{cos}t)(\operatorname{sin}t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{sin}^{2}t,2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}t,\operatorname{cos}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{'}(t) \\  & =⟨{sin}^{2}t,2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t⟩\cdot ⟨-\operatorname{sin}t,\operatorname{cos}t⟩ \\  & =-{sin}^{3}t+2\operatorname{sin}t{cos}^{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "673ff670-99f1-5416-aa83-5c4c8bf0e4f7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4967 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "87b55278-4bb6-5686-b4ef-178d5036b236" :step/math-academy-id 30935 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125318}} {:db/id 17592186125529 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124593 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124404 :question/id #uuid "c623bb85-401d-5d00-b4a8-cb86570d3304" :question/math-academy-id "e-8282"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cc017b0d-6418-570a-9a5d-57572e4fe70a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124956} {:db/id 17592186125246} {:db/id 17592186284585} {:db/id 17592186284586} {:db/id 17592186323880} {:db/id 17592186323883} {:db/id 17592186360524} {:db/id 17592186360525}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating the Derivative at a Point Using the Chain Rule"} :step/id #uuid "4850b0cc-54ab-5a26-9440-b0d1cf757680" :step/math-academy-id 30936 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125319}} {:db/id 17592186125530 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125836 :tutorial/content "The chain rule for a function $f(\mathbf{r}),$ where $\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle x_1(t), x_2(t), \ldots, x_m(t) \right\rangle$ is a vector-valued function of $m$ variables, is the same as before:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)
$$

How does this chain rule in vector form relate to the chain rule we have seen before, which states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d f} {\textrm d t} 	= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_1} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm d x_1}{\textrm d t}  
						+ \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_2} \cdot  \dfrac {\textrm d x_2}{\textrm d t} + \dots + \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_m} \cdot  \dfrac {\textrm d x_m}{\textrm d t}?

Let's expand $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)$ to see. Recall that

$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{'}(t)=⟨\frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{dt},\frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{dt},…,\frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{dt}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}},\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}},…,\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{dt},\frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{dt},…,\frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{dt}⟩ \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{\text{d}t}+⋯+\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

They are exactly the same, just different notations!

**Note**: If we replace $\mathbf{r}$ with a single-valued function $g(t),$ we get back the chain rule from single-variable calculus:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(g(t))] & =∇f(g(t))\cdot {g}^{'}(t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "15062cce-eede-545a-ae5d-e02432a0ba33" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4968 :tutorial/title "Intuition Behind the Vector Form of the Multivariable Chain Rule"} :step/id #uuid "fd19c878-fabf-5b99-9507-9a32fb862324" :step/math-academy-id 30937}] :activity/title "The Multivariable Chain Rule in Vector Form" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124728} {:db/id 17592186125528 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125835 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the function 

$$
f(\mathbf{r}) = f(x,y) = xy^2,
$$

which takes a vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle x(t), y(t) \right\rangle = \left\langle \cos t, \sin t \right\rangle
$$

as input. How do we calculate $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left[f(\mathbf{r}(t))\right]?$

To do this, we use the **multivariable chain rule in vector form**, which states

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left[f(\mathbf{r}(t))\right] = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot \mathbf{r}'(t).
$$

Let's now apply this to our functions. First, we compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(f(x,y)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(f(x,y))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨{y}^{2},2xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\cos t$ and $y=\sin t$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨(\operatorname{sin}t)^{2},2(\operatorname{cos}t)(\operatorname{sin}t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{sin}^{2}t,2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}t,\operatorname{cos}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{'}(t) \\  & =⟨{sin}^{2}t,2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t⟩\cdot ⟨-\operatorname{sin}t,\operatorname{cos}t⟩ \\  & =-{sin}^{3}t+2\operatorname{sin}t{cos}^{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "673ff670-99f1-5416-aa83-5c4c8bf0e4f7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4967 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "87b55278-4bb6-5686-b4ef-178d5036b236" :step/math-academy-id 30935 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125318}} {:db/id 17592186125318 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124469 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124276 :question/id #uuid "253b765d-be85-574e-8e32-c359ffbecdea" :question/math-academy-id "e-3694"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0096e314-e53e-5d9b-9cee-fe34fa3a6379" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048954} {:db/id 17592186048999} {:db/id 17592186050031}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124955} {:db/id 17592186125249} {:db/id 17592186323878} {:db/id 17592186360544} {:db/id 17592186360545} {:db/id 17592186360547}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Vector Form of the Chain Rule to a Function of Two Variables"} :step/id #uuid "2f62c8fc-daae-562a-a01e-851a375ec7a4" :step/math-academy-id 12678 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125320}} {:db/id 17592186125320 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124470 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124277 :question/id #uuid "033e459e-5148-5e78-ab5c-7e455b06cd64" :question/math-academy-id "e-3695"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "112e3378-bde8-5896-822e-e815bde51501" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124959} {:db/id 17592186125250} {:db/id 17592186284584} {:db/id 17592186360548} {:db/id 17592186360550} {:db/id 17592186360577} {:db/id 17592186360578} {:db/id 17592186360579}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Vector Form of the Chain Rule to a Function of Three Variables"} :step/id #uuid "ef0f7fd7-782e-55cb-8008-f28d770450ed" :step/math-academy-id 12682 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125529}} {:db/id 17592186125319 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125749 :tutorial/content "We can consider $f(\mathbf{r}(t))$ as the values taken by the function $f$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t).$ So, the derivative 

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))]
$$

can be interpreted as the **rate of change of $f$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t).$**

Furthermore, if $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is a level curve $f(x,y)=c,$ then by the chain rule we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =c \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(f(r(t))) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(c) \\ ∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{'}(t) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

[17592186046659 1007 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I develops the core mathematical structures and analytical tools used throughout theoretical and applied physics. Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.
Students learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.
Students then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.
The course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.
The course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations.
